floor_changes.why: Breaks the direct window-to-window line between the lower pair.

floor_changes.direction: a low colonnade toward the park edge
floor_changes.why: Answers the scale of the Art Deco and chawl edge around Shivaji Park.

hyb.whats_wrong: A single rounded tube in the middle of the plot. It has no overlooking problem and a very elegant proportion, but it gives up two-thirds of the yield the client asked for. The plate is also non-directional, so it does not favour the sea to the west. As a lone pencil it ignores the park-edge context.

floor_changes.amount: about 30% longer on the E-W axis
floor_changes.why: Adds sellable area on the sea-facing side.
Upper units get a sea view past the towers along the coast.
The tower needs a base that meets the maidan.

rows.reason: Marginally better proportion and a small top reduction, but both are boring.
rows.quote: Two extrusions. B is the less lazy one, and that's the nicest thing I can say.

win1.whats_wrong: A square rotated 45 degrees and extruded 80 floors with no change at all. It is efficient, but it has zero identity on one of the most visible skylines in the world. The corners point at the harbour but nothing is made of them.

floor_changes.direction: toward the harbour to the south-west as it rises
floor_changes.why: Gives a sculptural skyline presence and sweeps upper units toward the harbour.
It currently just stops at 288 m.
The low floors are hemmed in by neighbours, so outdoor rooms at the corner are the value.

hyb.whats_wrong: The same idea with the square turned about 30 degrees and the top slightly reduced. The proportion is a touch better, but it is still an extrusion. The rotation seems arbitrary and aims neither at the Hudson nor at the harbour.

floor_changes.direction: one face flat to the harbour to the south
floor_changes.why: If the plate stays square, at least one face should get the water.
Gives a sculptural taper and water-facing terraces.
Needs a skyline signature.

rows.reason: The rounded, twisting plate and the podium on the square give fairer views and fit the context better, though B needs to be taller and thinner.
rows.quote: Every flat should feel it's facing the park; B is starting to do that, A leaves the south corners in the dark.

win1.whats_wrong: A big diamond extruded to 151 m, well short of the allowed 295 m. The south and west corners crowd tall neighbours, while only the NE face gets the Bryant Park-style square. The corner flats facing the slab to the south-west get nothing, so view equity is poor.

floor_changes.direction: alternating boxes cantilevering toward the park to the north-east
floor_changes.why: Pixelates the diamond so more units reach the park, in the MVRDV and Safdie spirit.
There is height to spare, and the upper floors would clear the neighbours for all-round equity.

floor_changes.direction: away from the tall slab to the south-west
floor_changes.why: Close overlooking at the low floors.

hyb.whats_wrong: A soft rounded plate that twists slowly toward the park, on a podium that meets the square well. It stops at about 112 m, so it is squat for a Midtown supertall site, and the plate is too fat for slenderness. Even so, the rounded plan distributes view better than A's diamond.

floor_changes.why: The proportion is too stocky.

floor_changes.amount: add about 40 floors toward the 295 m limit
floor_changes.why: Clearing the midtown canyon is where view equity comes from.
Sky terraces shared across the upper units.

rows.reason: The podium and directional plate respond to the river and the street, and it is still a highly repeatable tower.
rows.quote: B gives the City a proper base and points its best rooms at the river; lovely, just mind the east side.

win1.whats_wrong: A regular octagon, repeated straight up to 187 m. It is well built and slender, and it is pushed to the SW corner of the site toward the Tower of London and the river. Its eight faces give equal glazing in every direction, including toward the office slabs to the north-east, where you look straight into offices.

floor_changes.direction: solid NE facets toward the office neighbours
floor_changes.why: Privacy from the office floors across the street.

floor_changes.direction: the SW facets toward the Thames and Tower Bridge
floor_changes.amount: a recessed winter garden every 3 floors
floor_changes.why: A Puri-style carved outdoor room that frames the river and stays repeatable.
Uses the remaining height and signals the top.

hyb.whats_wrong: An elongated chamfered plate on a proper podium. The long faces point roughly NNW to SSE, so the southern end looks at the river, and the base meets the medieval street edge. The long east face still overlooks the neighbour at close range, and the plan is a single unarticulated repeat.

floor_changes.direction: short end square to the Tower and Tower Bridge to the south
floor_changes.why: Better aims the narrow end units at the river.

floor_changes.direction: away from the building to the east
floor_changes.why: Privacy on the long east face and a repeatable facade system.
Adds river-facing loggias without breaking the repetition.

rows.reason: The stepping edges already carry the seed of verandahs and shade, though A must be made slimmer and taller.
rows.quote: A tower should breathe; A has the beginnings of verandahs, B is a beautiful sealed bottle.

hyb.whats_wrong: A wide chamfered plate with slab edges that step slightly in and out. I like that it begins to read as verandahs, a shaded threshold life. But it is squat at 108 m against a 140 m limit, the plate nearly fills the envelope, and the deep plan leaves dark centres. The dock water lies to the north-east, and the massing does not acknowledge it.

floor_changes.direction: the NE corner toward the dock
floor_changes.why: Doshi-like shared outdoor rooms that bring air and light into the deep plan.
The proportion is too stocky, and a thinner plan lets light into the centre.
Recovers the area removed by slimming.

win1.whats_wrong: A square that rotates about 30 degrees up to 133 m. The proportion is more slender and elegant, but it has smooth, sealed faces with no depth for shade or shared outdoor space. The rotation happens on every floor, which complicates repetition. The curved office tower to the east is close.

floor_changes.why: Gives three repeatable blocks, in the Foster discipline.

floor_changes.direction: toward the dock water to the north
floor_changes.amount: the triangular offcut left by each rotation step
floor_changes.why: The offcuts become shaded communal verandahs, a village in the sky.

floor_changes.direction: away from the curved tower to the east
floor_changes.why: Privacy at close range.

rows.reason: The cruciform self-shades, repeats and gives better privacy, and the facade is simpler to build.
rows.quote: The cross shades itself and I can panelise it; the twist is a facade contractor's nightmare.

hyb.whats_wrong: A square plate that twists about 45 degrees and back over 151 m. It is an attractive silhouette, but every floor needs a different curtain-wall unit and bracket geometry. The flush glass has no shading, so the south and west faces will overheat. The low floors look straight at the tall slab directly to the south-west.

floor_changes.direction: hold the orientation toward the dock and river to the west
floor_changes.why: Allows a repeatable unitised facade.

floor_changes.direction: vertical fins on the south and west faces
floor_changes.why: Solar shading and angled privacy from the neighbour.

floor_changes.direction: away from the slab to the south-west
floor_changes.why: The overlooking at the base is severe.

win1.whats_wrong: A cruciform plate with the upper stage stepped slightly. The re-entrant corners are good for self-shading and give flats at the arm ends a three-sided outlook. But the rendering shows the arms broken into ragged slab edges. The inner corners of the arms look into each other.

floor_changes.direction: arms toward the dock water to the north-west
floor_changes.why: The arm tips then catch the water.
Stops the flats in adjacent arms looking into each other.

floor_changes.direction: shorten the east and south arms
floor_changes.why: Gives a more slender finish and terraces for the roof units.

rows.reason: B has the warmer base and the more humane, sculpted edges; it needs to be taller and thinner.
rows.quote: A is a good pencil; B actually says hello to the street, and I'll take that.

win1.whats_wrong: A slender chamfered rectangle with slightly wobbling slab edges, rising to about 280 m. It is a fine skyline proportion. At street level it just lands on the plot with no public room, and the low floors sit against a huge slab tower to the east.

floor_changes.direction: open a plaza toward the avenue to the south
floor_changes.amount: a 12 m setback with a covered arcade
floor_changes.why: Heatherwick-style generosity to the Midtown street.

floor_changes.direction: away from the big tower to the east
floor_changes.why: Privacy close to the slab.
Planted cut-outs give views down the avenues and toward the rivers.

hyb.whats_wrong: A rounded, pebble-like plate with scalloped floor edges and a podium. It is friendlier and more sculptural, and the base engages the street. It stops at 234 m, well below the limit, and the plate is fat. The balcony undulation creates edges that look down onto the neighbours.

floor_changes.why: Strengthens the public realm that the podium already starts.
The proportion is heavier than it needs to be.
Upper floors clear the canyon toward the river views.

rows.reason: B's height gets above the canyon, and the evidence is in the rendering: more of the harbour is visible over the rooftops.
rows.quote: Height is the only view strategy that works on this block. B has it, but it still needs a reason to face the water.

hyb.whats_wrong: A squat chamfered octagon, only about 49 floors and 176 m against roughly 225 m allowed, sits wedged between much taller slabs. The plates wobble a little in rotation but never commit to the harbour to the NW, and the big grey tower right beside it to the east looks straight into the lower half.

floor_changes.amount: add about 12 floors to reach about 220 m
floor_changes.why: The only clear harbour sightline is above the neighbouring slabs.

floor_changes.direction: long face toward the harbour to the NW, blank short face to the slab on the east
floor_changes.why: It stops living rooms facing the adjacent tower from about 25 m away.
Shaded, west-facing harbour terraces, with a crown that reads within the Lower Manhattan setback tradition.

win1.whats_wrong: A taller, cleaner square prism at about 220 m and 61 floors that clears more of its neighbours. But it is an extrusion with no idea about climate or context: the square is set diagonally to the triangular site, so one corner points at the harbour and two faces look at the dense towers to the east and south.

floor_changes.direction: away from the tower to the east
floor_changes.amount: offset the plate 4 m to the west
floor_changes.why: The lower floors look into the neighbouring slab.
Recessed loggias shade the west glass and frame the water.
It echoes the setback crowns of the neighbouring towers.

rows.reason: The rotation distributes the sea and park views more fairly across the floors.
rows.quote: A tower in Bombay must breathe. A at least turns its head toward the sea.

win1.whats_wrong: There is a gentle twist from a diamond at the base to a near-orthogonal square at the top, so the upper flats swing toward the sea to the west and Shivaji Park. Every floor is a sealed square with no verandah or shaded void, which is wrong for Mumbai's monsoon and sun.

floor_changes.direction: SW and NW corners toward the sea and park
floor_changes.why: Correa's open-to-sky space gives every flat a shaded outdoor room facing the view.

floor_changes.direction: clockwise toward the sea to the west
floor_changes.why: The upper third should look squarely at the Arabian Sea.

hyb.whats_wrong: A static square prism at a fixed 15-degree skew. It is cheap and efficient, but the same flat is repeated 49 times, so view equity is fixed: the east-facing flats look at the city forever.

floor_changes.direction: toward the sea to the west
floor_changes.why: It gives the eastern flats a diagonal share of the sea.
They shade the afternoon sun and give privacy toward the lanes.

rows.reason: A's rotation is smoother, and both its proportion and its silhouette read better.
rows.quote: A has a lovely continuous curve. Now make it face the river it came for.

hyb.whats_wrong: A slender rectangular bar that rotates gradually through about 35 degrees until its long face points north-south at the top. The ribbon of slabs reads nicely, but the rotation turns the long face away from the Thames to the south at the upper levels.

floor_changes.direction: hold the long face toward the Thames to the south
floor_changes.amount: stop the rotation at about 15 degrees
floor_changes.why: It keeps the widest glazing on the river.

floor_changes.amount: a 1.2 m slab-edge overhang every 2 floors
floor_changes.why: The Studio Gang-style undulating edge shades the south sun.

win1.whats_wrong: A similar bar with a stiffer, more stepwise rotation, which reads as a stack of shifted boxes. It is less fluid and the top is equally unresolved.

floor_changes.why: One continuous gesture gives a better silhouette.
It slims the crown against the cluster.

rows.reason: B's rotation is consistent and its elongated plate is oriented toward the open views.
rows.quote: B's rotation is coherent. A's is noise. Tie every degree to a sightline.

hyb.whats_wrong: A rounded polygon that rotates floor by floor. It is slender, but the rotation looks arbitrary rather than tracking the Thames bend, and the chamfers give it no solar shading.

floor_changes.direction: long axis toward the river to the south and east
floor_changes.why: Measured sightlines should drive the rotation, not form-making.
They cut solar gain and keep the flats private from the adjacent tower.

win1.whats_wrong: An elongated chamfered octagon that rotates progressively and consistently. It is a MAD-like, fluid read, but floor-to-floor heights look compressed at about 3.6 m, and the top is blunt.

floor_changes.why: It gives a softer crown and reduces wind load.

floor_changes.direction: toward the street to the north
floor_changes.why: It improves the public realm and the wind at street level.

rows.reason: Two slim towers are better spaced and have more privacy than three.
rows.quote: Two slender pencils beat three stubby boxes. B is the scheme for Dadar.

win1.whats_wrong: The plans show three chamfered-square towers, even though only two were expected at 24 m apart, and they appear tightly clustered in the aerial. The two eastern towers overlook each other, and the plates are near-identical extrusions.

floor_changes.why: The towers are too close for privacy.

floor_changes.direction: west tower toward the sea to the NW, east tower toward the park
floor_changes.why: No flats face each other directly.

hyb.whats_wrong: Two slim rounded towers well spaced on a diagonal, which gives a better slenderness ratio and silhouette. The west tower still partly blocks the east tower's sea view, and the extrusion has no variation.

floor_changes.why: The east tower clears the west tower's shadow toward the sea.
Skyline identity.

rows.reason: The twin slender towers read calmer against the harbour and give better flats. With a permeable base they would be very good.
rows.quote: A belongs to the water. B is shouting at it.

hyb.whats_wrong: Twin slender rounded towers on a podium at the harbour edge, with good spacing and open water views. The podium is heavy and blind to the esplanade, and the twin extrusions are identical and very tall for the Battery context.

floor_changes.direction: toward the esplanade and park to the west
floor_changes.amount: break the podium into two pavilions with a 15 m passage
floor_changes.why: A Piano-like permeable ground plane.

floor_changes.direction: away from each other, NW and SE
floor_changes.why: Removes the tower-to-tower sightline and opens the harbour view.
Shades the water-reflected afternoon sun.

win1.whats_wrong: A single triangular prism that rotates through about 60 degrees. It is a bold silhouette with total privacy, but the triangle's acute corners give poor flats, and a single 256 m spike on the park edge is out of scale with the waterfront.

floor_changes.why: Usable plans and less wind.
It relates better to the Battery edge.

rows.reason: B's taper and chamfered corners sell better views and read as a supertall.
rows.quote: B is a product. A is a spreadsheet with windows.

win1.whats_wrong: A plain square extrusion set 25 degrees off grid, the same at every floor. It is efficient to sell, but there is no premium differentiation up the height, and the lower half is hemmed in by Midtown slabs.

floor_changes.direction: toward the park and river to the NW
floor_changes.why: The Heatherwick-style gardens create premium units and a skyline identity.
Differentiates the lower stock.

hyb.whats_wrong: A chamfered octagon that tapers at the top to a slimmer crown. It is more elegant and marketable, but the lower floors still face neighbours closely and the taper happens only at the very top.

floor_changes.why: Penthouse-grade corner views over a longer run of floors.
Low-floor units have poor views and privacy.

rows.reason: The two drawings are the same scheme, so there is nothing to choose.
rows.quote: You showed me the same tower twice. Neither one has met the street.

hyb.whats_wrong: A fat rectangular bar that rotates about 45 degrees up the height and ends at 130 m. It does nothing at street level, and at the base the site is simply a hard apron.

floor_changes.direction: toward the lanes to the south and west
floor_changes.amount: a lifted undercroft or shaded public court
floor_changes.why: In the Doshi manner, give the ground back to the city.

floor_changes.direction: toward the Tower and the Thames to the south
floor_changes.why: The rotation should serve the river.
Too deep for single-aspect flats.

win1.whats_wrong: It is identical to A in every render and plan. The same problems apply: a deep plate, arbitrary rotation and a dead ground plane.

floor_changes.why: It serves the public realm.

floor_changes.amount: step every 7 floors rather than every floor
floor_changes.why: Fewer unique floor plates for similar effect.

rows.reason: The balcony banding and slight rotation give better facade depth and a better view angle.
rows.quote: B at least has a facade that talks. A is just a box beside a maidan.

win1.whats_wrong: A straight rectangular extrusion aligned to the park diagonal. It turns its long face to Shivaji Park but has no articulation, and the bland base does not respond to the busy junction.

floor_changes.direction: toward the park to the north
floor_changes.why: The BIG-style pixelated balconies catch the park and sea views.
Heritage continuity with the Dadar arcades.

hyb.whats_wrong: A near-square plate with a slight twist and visible balcony banding, which gives a livelier facade. It is still squat, and the corner does not engage the park directly.

floor_changes.direction: toward the park and the sea to the NW
floor_changes.why: More flats get the park view.
A public-facing crown terrace.

rows.reason: One tower that turns gives every flat its piece of the sea and nobody looks in. B makes neighbours out of its own residents.
rows.quote: If a building only works for half its flats, it doesn't work. A at least tries to be fair to all of them.

win1.whats_wrong: A single rounded-triangle tower that slowly rotates is generous: every flat gets a share of sea to the west and Shivaji Park to the east, and nobody on site looks into it. But the rotation is timid and the plate is still a blunt triangle, so the flats on the south-east point stare at low rooftops rather than the sea.

floor_changes.direction: turn the long face toward the Arabian Sea to the west-northwest
floor_changes.amount: about 15 degrees more by the top
floor_changes.why: so the upper flats get a straight-on sea view instead of an oblique one

floor_changes.direction: on the south-east tip facing the low-rise
floor_changes.why: lower flats see little; a shared garden gives them outlook and light
a lighter crown and terraces for the top units, in the spirit of Piano

hyb.whats_wrong: Two octagonal towers of different heights sit on the diagonal of the triangle, so the north tower blocks part of the sea view from the south tower and the facing sides look straight into each other. View equity breaks down: the south tower's flats on the north-west side face a wall.

floor_changes.direction: turn the facing sides away from each other, north tower toward the NW and south tower toward the SW
floor_changes.why: to stop flats looking straight into each other and open diagonal sea views

floor_changes.direction: push the north tower up to the northern tip
floor_changes.why: more distance means more privacy and less shadow on the lower tower
to lift the south tower's upper flats above the north tower's shadow toward the sea

rows.reason: They are the same idea; B's base fits the street better and A's twist opens the top faster. Neither deals with shading.
rows.quote: Two versions of the same twisted box. I would take B's feet and A's head, then give it some shade.

hyb.whats_wrong: A square plate that twists about 45 degrees over 194 m. It reads well in the Canary Wharf cluster, but it is hemmed in by big slabs to the south and east, and the twist is distributed evenly rather than tuned toward the Thames to the north. It has no shading response at all: a square glass box turning in the sun.

floor_changes.direction: toward the dock edge and street
floor_changes.why: to tie into the dockside grain and shade the pedestrian edge

floor_changes.direction: lock the corner toward the Thames to the north
floor_changes.amount: hold the rotation at 30 degrees through these floors
floor_changes.why: so mid-height flats see past the adjacent slab toward the river

floor_changes.amount: deep fins or recessed loggias 1.2 m
floor_changes.why: solar shading on the exposed faces, as Nouvel would layer it

win1.whats_wrong: Almost the same twisting square, but it starts aligned with the street grid at the base, which I appreciate for context. The rotation is slightly gentler, so the lower floors face straight into the neighbouring slab to the east.

floor_changes.why: to open diagonal glimpses to the river past the neighbouring towers

floor_changes.amount: set back 4 m over the top 4 floors
floor_changes.why: gives terraces and a crown that answers the cluster skyline
climate response on the unshaded sides

rows.reason: On the evidence of the section, A gets above the canyon and B does not. Slenderness buys the view here.
rows.quote: B is a fine building for 1960. A is the Midtown tower. Now make its rotation mean something.

win1.whats_wrong: A very slender chamfered plate rising to 310 m that tapers and turns slightly. The proportion is excellent, and at that height it clears most of Midtown to the rivers. The drift of the plate's orientation looks arbitrary rather than tuned to the Hudson to the west, and with a plate that small the core will eat the floor.

floor_changes.direction: long face toward the Hudson to the west
floor_changes.why: consistent river views for the upper half, where the premium lies

floor_changes.direction: open wind slots through the plate
floor_changes.why: to cut vortex shedding on a tower this slender
low-angle solar gain on a very exposed shaft

hyb.whats_wrong: A straight rotated-square extrusion stopping at about 234 m, pushed into the west corner of the triangle. It is easy to build but it is squat for Midtown, its upper floors stay among neighbouring towers, and the floors below 30 look into the neighbouring blocks.

floor_changes.amount: about 20 floors, toward the 315 m limit
floor_changes.why: to clear the surrounding towers and reach the river views
better slenderness and more corner flats
to lighten the top and reduce wind load

rows.reason: B has a sculpted character that sits gently in the medieval grain. A is an efficient diagram with no form to it.
rows.quote: B has a hand in it; A has a spreadsheet in it. Lean B toward the river and it will earn its site.

win1.whats_wrong: A trefoil or Y plan extruded unchanged to 101 m. The three wings give plenty of corner flats and aspects, but it is the same plate on every floor, so the silhouette is stiff. Its hard angular geometry does not answer the curved medieval lanes around it.

floor_changes.why: to answer the curved streets and soften the corners

floor_changes.direction: rotate the wings toward the Thames to the south
floor_changes.amount: about 20 degrees over the top 12 floors
floor_changes.why: to get the upper flats looking at the river instead of rooftops

floor_changes.amount: hold the street line up to 4 storeys
floor_changes.why: to keep the historic street wall intact

hyb.whats_wrong: A rounded square whose plates swell and pinch floor by floor, giving a tactile, stacked-pebble silhouette. Its soft form sits well among the City's curved lanes. But the plan is compact and centred, so it makes no specific move toward the Thames, and the varying slabs will cost money.

floor_changes.why: to push upper flats out toward the river views

floor_changes.amount: repeat 3 slab edges rather than every floor unique
floor_changes.why: keeps the form while cutting formwork cost
a crown with outdoor space facing the river

rows.reason: A gives the street a podium and the top a finish. B is cheap and has nothing else going for it.
rows.quote: B is a lift core wearing glass. A at least knows where the ground is. Strip out the wobble.

hyb.whats_wrong: A chamfered square that twists slightly, with a proper podium and a stepped top at 144 m. The podium gives the park and street an edge, which is right. The wobbling slab edges add cost for no clear gain, and the big slab to the east blocks the lower half's views regardless.

floor_changes.why: repetition pays for everything else; the twist buys nothing below the neighbour's roofline

floor_changes.direction: toward the dock and Thames to the north-west
floor_changes.why: spend the geometry where there is actually a view

floor_changes.direction: open onto the park to the east
floor_changes.why: make the ground floor serve the park

win1.whats_wrong: A plain rotated rectangle extruded to 144 m with no podium. Constructable, yes, but it lands on the plaza with no base, and it holds the same orientation at every floor even though the neighbouring tower blocks one long face.

floor_changes.amount: 4 storey base to the building line
floor_changes.why: no public realm otherwise
a top that finishes the tower

floor_changes.direction: away from the tall slab to the east
floor_changes.why: to stop the east flats looking into the neighbour

rows.reason: Fewer towers, but each one breathes and has a view. In Dadar, the neighbourhood reads B more easily.
rows.quote: Three towers is a count, not a design. B lets both towers see the sea without seeing into each other.

win1.whats_wrong: Three similar towers placed along the diagonal. The northern and southern ones sit at the water edges, but the middle one looks straight at the other two. View equity fails for the middle tower, and the south-facing flats of the north tower look into the middle one.

floor_changes.direction: turn the middle tower's plate to face west to the sea
floor_changes.why: so the middle tower's flats look out between the others rather than into them

floor_changes.direction: vary heights: north tower lowest, middle tallest
floor_changes.why: stepped heights give every tower a line to the sea, MVRDV-style
to turn overlooking faces into shared outdoor rooms

hyb.whats_wrong: Two towers, further apart and offset on the diagonal, giving much less overlooking, a lighter footprint and more open ground. But the north-west tower still blocks the sea view for the south-east tower on the lower floors.

floor_changes.why: to see past the other tower toward the bay
to lift its upper flats above the other tower

floor_changes.direction: link the two towers at ground
floor_changes.why: to give the neighbourhood a shared, shaded ground

rows.reason: A starts the gesture that B never makes. Both need a skin, but A has a form worth wrapping.
rows.quote: B is a pencil. A is a pencil that knows where the river is. Twist it harder.

hyb.whats_wrong: A slender elongated octagon to 310 m with a gradual rotation. It sits on the East River waterfront with big water views. The rotation is too subtle to read, and the plate has no shading or skin variation, even though its long face turns into the western sun.

floor_changes.direction: toward the harbour to the south
floor_changes.why: so the rotation reads as a form and lines the top floors up with the harbour

floor_changes.amount: vertical fins 0.5-0.8 m, varying with height
floor_changes.why: shading and a SHoP-like textured skin
a crown that answers the Lower Manhattan skyline

win1.whats_wrong: An almost unchanging octagon to 295 m. It is equally slender, but the plate is compact and small, so it says nothing to the river it stands next to. It is the neutral version.

floor_changes.direction: long face toward the East River and bridges
floor_changes.why: the bridges are the view; face them
to push corner flats out over the water views
climate response

rows.reason: B has a base and a taper; A has neither. Both ignore the sun.
rows.quote: A is an extrusion, not a design. B at least has a foot and a shoulder. Neither has a sunshade, which is lazy.

win1.whats_wrong: A rotated square extruded unchanged to 310 m. It is easy to build and slender enough, but there is no base, no top and no shading. The rotation off the Manhattan grid points the corners at the neighbours rather than at either river.

floor_changes.why: Midtown needs a streetwall; this lands like a pin
to reduce wind loads and give a top
shading built into the section, not bolted on

hyb.whats_wrong: A rectangle that tapers slightly, over a real base. The podium is the right call and the gentle taper helps with wind. But its long faces still aim at the neighbouring towers, not at the Hudson or East River, and there is still no climate response.

floor_changes.direction: long face east-west toward both rivers
floor_changes.why: to align the long faces with the two rivers
wind at 310 m
shading

rows.reason: A is humbler and softer against its neighbours. B's height gives it nothing it could not get by opening up.
rows.quote: Neither touches the ground properly. A at least speaks quietly. Give it verandahs and a street edge.

hyb.whats_wrong: A soft rounded plate that twists gently up to 140 m, beside the tracks and a highway. The height is more modest and the form is more civil, but it lands on a hard triangle with no public ground, no shaded threshold, and no verandah or deep openings for a climate that deserves them.

floor_changes.direction: toward the park and street to the north
floor_changes.why: the ground floor must serve the street, not just the lobby
outdoor rooms and shade, Doshi-style

floor_changes.direction: toward the Thames to the south
floor_changes.why: to aim the upper flats at the water

win1.whats_wrong: A rotated square extruded to 191 m. Its floors have visible ledges that look like balconies, which is a start. But it is taller and blunter against the surrounding low-rise, and its corner pointed at the tracks does nothing for the street.

floor_changes.why: to sit better with the low-rise neighbourhood to the north
a public edge

floor_changes.amount: cut 3 m by 3 m every 5 floors
floor_changes.why: to give shaded outdoor rooms facing the water

floor_changes.amount: a 3-stage stepped chamfer of 3 m each
floor_changes.why: A 285 m tower needs a recognisable top, and the premium flats pay for it.

floor_changes.amount: a double-height recessed loggia every 5 floors
floor_changes.why: Self-shading on the hot facade and a signature pattern.

win1.whats_wrong: A square that twists about 45 degrees over its height. The corners turn progressively toward the park and river diagonals, which gives more identity than A. The plan shrinks slightly at mid-height, then grows at the top. The flat faces offer no shading.

floor_changes.why: The lower half barely turns and loses the diagonal views between neighbouring towers.
Wind shedding on a slender twist, and corner living rooms.
Solar shading that also reinforces the twist.

rows.reason: Its stacking already hints at terraces and shade; with deeper shifts it could give every flat a garden.
rows.quote: B has the beginnings of a verandah tower in Manhattan. Make the shifts brave.

win1.whats_wrong: A slender rectangle twisting about 60 degrees, hemmed in by big neighbours at close range. The twist is a nice gesture, but the long faces still stare across narrow Midtown streets into offices. There is no balcony or shading anywhere, and it ignores the tower-podium rhythm of the street.

floor_changes.direction: flush to the avenue street wall
floor_changes.why: Holds the street line the way its neighbours do.

floor_changes.direction: the corners that face the gaps between towers
floor_changes.why: Outdoor space and shade where the outlook is actually open.

floor_changes.direction: away from the tall tower close to the east
floor_changes.why: Pushes the long faces away from facing windows.

hyb.whats_wrong: Stacked, slightly shifted boxes with a notched corner at the lower floors. The texture is more Heatherwick, and the notch could hold terraces, but the shifts are too small to give real outdoor space. The top half becomes a plain rotated square.

floor_changes.direction: alternating toward the avenue view corridors
floor_changes.why: Makes real planted terraces out of the stacking.
Keeps the outdoor rooms going to the top.

rows.reason: A is more considered in form and its banding; B is a stock block with a hat.
rows.quote: A has a form; B has a floor plate and a hat.

win1.whats_wrong: The chamfered hexagon plate with recessed banding every few floors reads crisply. But it stays roughly the same size up to 104 m, and it faces a big neighbour close by to the SE. The long diagonal faces give uneven views.

floor_changes.direction: away from the large tower to the SE
floor_changes.why: Stops the lower flats looking straight into office glazing.
Equalises the views and makes the upper silhouette.

hyb.whats_wrong: A rotated square that is a plain block to about floor 23, then steps in abruptly with slabs at the top. The top works, but the shaft is stocky and generic, and corner flats point their diagonals toward the neighbours.

floor_changes.why: More distance from the SE neighbour, and a better proportion.

floor_changes.direction: alternating plate offsets in the MVRDV manner
floor_changes.why: Gives each flat a distinct outlook and breaks up the block.

rows.reason: More corner units and diagonal outlooks spread the views more evenly across the flats.
rows.quote: Count the corners: B gives eight flats a diagonal, A gives four.

win1.whats_wrong: A near-square extrusion with a slight rotation and no change in section. Its faces sit hard against the supertall to its NE, and nothing shades the south or west faces. Flats on the NE side get a wall of office glass.

floor_changes.direction: diagonal toward the avenue corridor and the park to the N
floor_changes.why: Looks down the street gaps rather than at facades.
Shading, plus a view pocket for the corner flats.

hyb.whats_wrong: A chamfered octagon plate that rotates slightly and tapers, then widens at the top. The octagon gives more corner units with diagonal views, which is fairer, but the mid-height shrink costs floor area for no clear gain.

floor_changes.why: The pinch does not buy any view.
Climate response for the exposed faces.

rows.reason: The chamfers spread the views fairly without hurting efficiency.
rows.quote: The octagon is the honest compromise: every flat gets a corner of the river.

hyb.whats_wrong: An octagonal plate on the triangle site, rotating gently and set well back from the edges, so it is private. From the opposite aerial the river is directly south. The plate is compact, and the chamfers suit a unitised facade. But it sits back toward the site's SW rather than making the most of the river frontage.

floor_changes.direction: a flat face toward the Thames to the S
floor_changes.why: More flats square-on to the river.
A light top in the manner of Piano.

win1.whats_wrong: A plain square that rotates to follow the site. It is efficient, but a square plan gives four corner flats and deep mid-units with a weaker share of the view. It reads as an anonymous extrusion.

floor_changes.why: More glazing on the diagonals, and view equity.

floor_changes.direction: toward the river to the S
floor_changes.why: The rotation currently follows the site, not the view.

rows.reason: A is a real skyline figure; B is a tube.
rows.quote: Next to One World Trade, a tube is not enough. A at least has a body.

hyb.whats_wrong: A soft superellipse plate that swells and slims toward a tapered crown. It is a good sculptural object at 300 m next to One WTC. But the ground plane is ignored: the tower lands in the plaza with no podium or colonnade, and the sinuous plates cost money.

floor_changes.direction: opening onto the plaza to the E
floor_changes.why: The public realm deserves a gesture.

floor_changes.direction: toward the Hudson to the W
floor_changes.why: Leans the premium floors toward the water.

win1.whats_wrong: The same rounded square extruded from bottom to top. It is buildable and slender, but it adds nothing to the skyline and ignores both the Hudson and the plaza.

floor_changes.why: Gives it a silhouette.
Street life.

rows.reason: A has a stronger outlook, B has the better efficiency; neither is quite there yet.
rows.quote: One is too restless and one too vague. I'd take A's aim and B's discipline.

win1.whats_wrong: Rectangular plates rotate about 50 degrees in stacked blocks with visible shifts. The composition is lively, but it clashes with the calm Canary Wharf grid, and the shifting slabs complicate transfer structures.

floor_changes.amount: limit the rotation to about 20 degrees
floor_changes.why: Respects the Canary Wharf context and simplifies the core.

floor_changes.direction: long face toward the park and docks to the N
floor_changes.why: Views over the green to the north.

hyb.whats_wrong: A chamfered octagon plate that rotates slightly and wobbles in outline. It is calmer than A, but the wavy silhouette reads as indecisive, and the plate shrinks at the top.

floor_changes.amount: one plate with less than 1 m variation
floor_changes.why: Plan efficiency and repeat formwork.
Upper terraces facing the green.

rows.reason: A spreads the rotation over the whole height, so more flats get a fair diagonal outlook.
rows.quote: A turns from the ground up; B wakes up halfway.

win1.whats_wrong: A slender rectangle rotating about 45 degrees to 299 m. It is a SHoP-like elegance, and the upper floors turn toward the diagonal gaps. But it sits right next to a huge slab tower to the east, and the lower long faces look straight into it.

floor_changes.direction: away from the big slab tower to the E
floor_changes.why: Privacy for the lower half.
A defined top.

hyb.whats_wrong: A narrow N-S rectangle that only starts rotating above floor 45. The lower half's short faces look at nothing, and its long faces face the neighbours across the street.

floor_changes.amount: start the rotation at floor 6, about 0.5 degrees per floor
floor_changes.why: The lower flats need the diagonal outlook too.

rows.reason: The rotating plates at least try to give each flat its own outlook past the neighbours.
rows.quote: Every family deserves a window that isn't a wall. B is the start of that, A isn't.

hyb.whats_wrong: A plain square extrusion jammed right up against a huge slab to the east. Half the flats look straight at a blank grey wall and nobody gets the docks. The ground floor gives nothing back to the plaza.

floor_changes.direction: turn the long faces NW/SE, away from the slab to the east
floor_changes.why: so no flat's main room faces the neighbouring wall head-on

floor_changes.direction: stepping down toward the open plaza to the SW
floor_changes.why: Safdie-style terraces give each flat sky and a garden

floor_changes.direction: open to the plaza on the south
floor_changes.why: give the street back

win1.whats_wrong: The rotating plate is a good idea because corners slide past the slab and every flat gets a different angle. But the rotation is timid and uneven, and the east flats in the lower floors still stare at the wall.

floor_changes.direction: away from the slab to the east
floor_changes.why: more distance for the lower flats that suffer most

floor_changes.direction: on the NW and SW corners
floor_changes.why: view equity: shared outdoor rooms with a long view

rows.reason: The diagonal plates face outward and avoid the flats looking into each other while keeping the plans efficient.
rows.quote: B is a family of towers. A is a car park of them.

hyb.whats_wrong: Three identical rectangular slabs with some stagger. The plans are efficient, but the long faces of the central and western towers partly face each other, and the skyline reads as a generic triplet.

floor_changes.direction: step each crown at a different height toward the river NE
floor_changes.why: a skyline identity instead of three equal sticks

floor_changes.direction: splay the west tower away from the centre one
floor_changes.why: remove the facing long walls

win1.whats_wrong: The plates are turned diagonally, so the narrow ends face each other and the long faces look outward, and the slight articulation reads better. The heights are still too uniform and the plans could be tighter around the cores.

floor_changes.direction: toward the Thames to the NE
floor_changes.amount: 1.5 m per floor on the river face
floor_changes.why: a sculpted skyline and a larger top for the premium river view
a graded group with a clear lead tower

rows.reason: At least A's stagger can be turned into balconies. B has nothing to work with.
rows.quote: Neither gives a flat a balcony. A just pretends better.

hyb.whats_wrong: The staggered floors are decoration without purpose. There are no real balconies, and the huge site is left empty with no public ground.

floor_changes.why: real outdoor rooms for every flat, not a textured skin

floor_changes.amount: a public court at street level
floor_changes.why: the empty site should serve the street

win1.whats_wrong: A dumb box with zero outdoor space and no gesture to the river. It is easy to build and that is all it is.

floor_changes.direction: on the SW corner facing the river
floor_changes.amount: a 4x4 m cut-out on every floor
floor_changes.why: outdoor space per flat
to earn the river view

rows.reason: A's form responds to its context, and I would rather adjust its height than soften B's crude extrusion.
rows.quote: The data might favour B's height, but the street will favour A.

hyb.whats_wrong: The soft rounded plan with a tapered top is elegant and cuts overlooking. But it is short and the pinched crown loses floor area, while the water to the east is barely engaged. The base on the roundabout does nothing.

floor_changes.amount: about 3 m over the top 12 floors
floor_changes.why: give the upper flats the water view

floor_changes.direction: toward the pedestrian route to the SW
floor_changes.why: public realm

win1.whats_wrong: It reaches 209 m and captures the water, but it is a relentless square extrusion that is out of scale with the low residential blocks around it.

floor_changes.direction: all sides, more on the west toward the low housing
floor_changes.why: reduce bulk against the neighbouring terraces
softer silhouette and wider view cones

rows.reason: The two are essentially the same scheme, and both need a climate layer.
rows.quote: Two good straight lines. Now let's give them a verandah.

hyb.whats_wrong: Two rotated square towers with a notch near the top of one. They are repetitive and buildable. There is no shading strategy, and the towers are set diagonally so some corners look at each other.

floor_changes.direction: deep balconies on the south and west faces
floor_changes.why: shading against the western sun, and outdoor rooms

floor_changes.direction: offset the crowns of the two towers
floor_changes.why: variety on the skyline without extra cost

win1.whats_wrong: It is almost identical to A with a slightly different crown step. The same issue applies: glass boxes with no climatic depth.

floor_changes.direction: rotate the southern tower away from the northern one
floor_changes.why: reduce the corner-to-corner overlooking
a repetitive shading element that is cheap

rows.reason: The chamfers give more flats a diagonal view to the water.
rows.quote: A has the seeds of a sky-village. B is a filing cabinet.

win1.whats_wrong: A chamfered octagon squeezed between tall towers. The dock view to the south opens, but the flats to the east and north face big neighbours, and the skyline identity is weak.

floor_changes.why: Correa-style open-to-sky terraces facing the water

floor_changes.direction: the NE corner facing the tower
floor_changes.why: air and privacy where the neighbour is close

hyb.whats_wrong: A generic square box on a plinth. It turns a flat face to the neighbours, and nothing marks it on the skyline.

floor_changes.why: widen the view cones past the neighbours
an identity on the skyline

rows.reason: On this skyline A's identity sells, but the twist needs to be tamed for cost.
rows.quote: The twist is the brand. Just don't let it bankrupt the facade package.

win1.whats_wrong: The twisting single tower is a strong skyline object and it sweeps through the views. But a twist of about 90 degrees on a small plate costs cladding money, and it drops the second tower. With no shading, the south faces overheat.

floor_changes.amount: reduce to about 60 degrees in total
floor_changes.why: cut the facade cost and keep the sculptural read
self-shading

hyb.whats_wrong: Two slim towers on a large podium give more sellable area and are straightforward to build, but they are anonymous. The towers are close enough on the diagonal to overlook each other.

floor_changes.why: an identity, and the pair turns away from each other

floor_changes.direction: a green roof on the podium facing south
floor_changes.why: climate and amenity

rows.reason: It is buildable in Mumbai conditions, and verandahs can be added to it without losing the repetition.
rows.quote: In Dadar you build what the contractor can repeat. B, with verandahs.

hyb.whats_wrong: The rotating square turns toward the sea and Shivaji Park, which is good. But the rotation changes every floor, which breaks the repetition of the formwork, and there are no verandahs for monsoon living.

floor_changes.amount: rotate in 4 blocks of about 12 floors each
floor_changes.why: formwork repetition within each block
outdoor space and shade from the western sun

win1.whats_wrong: A diamond plan with its corners facing the sea is simple and repeats perfectly. But it has no outdoor space and a flat top.

floor_changes.direction: the west corner facing the sea
floor_changes.amount: a 3 m recessed balcony on every floor
floor_changes.why: outdoor space per flat within the same repeated plate
sea-view terraces

rows.reason: The plate is more efficient and easier to sculpt with balconies.
rows.quote: Give me B's plate and A's ambition: a square that opens up to the river.

hyb.whats_wrong: A small octagonal plate with a wobbly stagger and a pinched top. It is too skinny for an efficient plan, and it squanders a large site at only 104 m with little river view.

floor_changes.direction: toward the Thames to the south
floor_changes.why: better plan efficiency
Doshi-style outdoor rooms with a view of the river

win1.whats_wrong: A clean square that slightly flares at the top. It is efficient but mute, and it has no outdoor space.

floor_changes.why: outdoor space and shade

floor_changes.direction: toward the river bend to the SW
floor_changes.why: a form that points to the view

rows.reason: It is repetitive, buildable and taller. B wastes the height envelope.
rows.quote: Show me the formwork cycle first. A has one, B has twenty.

win1.whats_wrong: A rotated square extrusion reaching about 122 m, well under the 185 m allowed. The plate is the same on every floor, which is good for the formwork, but none of the faces is turned squarely to the Arabian Sea to the west, and there is no shading depth on the west and south faces for the afternoon sun.

floor_changes.direction: turn one long face to the sea to the W/NW
floor_changes.amount: about 15 degrees, as one fixed rotation (not a twist)
floor_changes.why: Gives a full elevation of sea view while keeping one repeated plate for the formwork.
Self-shading against the afternoon sun and monsoon rain, and outdoor space.

floor_changes.amount: add about 14 floors up to roughly 170 m
floor_changes.why: The upper floors clear the low-rise Dadar fabric and see the whole sea horizon.

hyb.whats_wrong: A rounded, tapering plate that stops at about 72 m, so it gives away most of the permitted height. The curved slab edges change on every floor, which means non-repetitive formwork, and the tapered stub reads squat against the sea.

floor_changes.why: At 72 m the building sits at the height of its neighbours and loses the sea.

floor_changes.amount: change the plate every 8 floors instead of every floor
floor_changes.why: Repetition keeps the cost down.

rows.reason: The chamfers share out the views more fairly. Both designs still need verandahs.
rows.quote: A tower in Mumbai without a verandah is a tower designed in London.

win1.whats_wrong: A chamfered octagon that necks in around the middle floors and widens again near the top. The chamfered corners spread views more evenly between flats, but there are no verandahs or deep shading, and the waist costs area without giving any flat a better view.

floor_changes.direction: W and SW chamfers facing Shivaji Park and the sea
floor_changes.amount: double-height verandahs every 3 floors, 3 m deep
floor_changes.why: In the Doshi tradition: shaded in-between space, cross-ventilation and a view for every flat.

floor_changes.direction: toward the sea to the NW
floor_changes.why: Opens sky terraces facing the sea for the upper flats.

hyb.whats_wrong: A plain rotated square rising 166 m without variation. The corner flats get the park and the sea, while the flats in the middle of each face look straight at the city. There is no climate response.

floor_changes.why: More flats get a diagonal view, and wind loads come down.
West sun.

rows.reason: It gives the tower an identity while the plan stays fairly efficient.
rows.quote: B is a spreadsheet. A at least attempts a silhouette.

hyb.whats_wrong: A chamfered hexagon that tapers gently to about 133 m. It has a decent crown, but the long axis runs NW-SE and misses the docks, and the plan loses efficiency at the obtuse corners.

floor_changes.direction: toward the docks and the Thames to the NE
floor_changes.why: MVRDV-style pixel shifts give the tower an identity and frame the water.

floor_changes.amount: an open sky garden 2 floors high
floor_changes.why: A skyline marker for the Wharf cluster.

win1.whats_wrong: A generic square extrusion. The plan is efficient, but the tower has no identity among the Canary Wharf boxes.

floor_changes.direction: toward the river to the N
floor_changes.why: Sculptural character, and cantilevered corner flats with water views.

rows.reason: The splayed plates deal with the two towers overlooking each other and keep a repeatable structure.
rows.quote: The angle does the work. Keep the floor-to-floor cycle and add shade.

win1.whats_wrong: Two identical square prisms about 176 m tall, with parallel faces looking into each other across the site. The south tower blocks part of the north tower's sea view, and neither tower has any shading.

floor_changes.direction: south tower away from the north tower, turned to the W sea
floor_changes.why: Stops the flats looking into each other and opens the sea view.
The Correa-style climate buffer for the afternoon sun.

hyb.whats_wrong: The rotated rectangular plates already splay the two towers apart, and the top slims down. The rectangles are narrow, though, so the cores will be tight, and there is still nothing for shade.

floor_changes.direction: toward the Arabian Sea to the W
floor_changes.why: Shaded terraces facing the sea at the upper levels.
Correa's open-to-sky space at the base.

rows.reason: The difference is only the corner radius. Both have the same problem where the two towers face each other.
rows.quote: These are the same building with different fillets. Fix the gap, not the radius.

hyb.whats_wrong: Two rounded towers of different heights, placed diagonally. The flats on the facing sides get a view of the other tower instead of the river, and the plan shapes differ slightly between the two towers.

floor_changes.direction: both long faces to the Thames to the N
floor_changes.why: Every flat gets a share of the river.
Less overlooking between the facing flats.

win1.whats_wrong: It is practically the same scheme as A with slightly rounder corners. The same flats in the gap between the towers look at each other.

floor_changes.direction: both towers turned away from each other
floor_changes.why: View equity for the inward-facing flats.

rows.reason: The wings give the privacy and the slenderness this site deserves.
rows.quote: B has a spine and a soul; A is a pillar standing on a pedestal.

hyb.whats_wrong: A chunky octagon rising from a heavy podium to about 184 m. The podium makes the base feel squat, and the flat faces look straight onto the neighbouring blocks.

floor_changes.why: The tower should touch the ground lightly.
Proportion.

win1.whats_wrong: A Y-shaped, three-wing plate that twists slowly. The wings shield the flats from each other and from the neighbours, but the reentrant corners can overlook each other on the lower floors.

floor_changes.amount: open the wing angle by 10 degrees
floor_changes.why: Privacy in the reentrant corners.
A sharper, more elegant finish at the top.

rows.reason: Three smaller towers are more humane and can take terraces. B is a corporate shaft.
rows.quote: Give every family a garden in the sky, and A is where to start.

hyb.whats_wrong: Three rounded towers in a line along the narrow site. Only the southern tower sees the Thames in full, and the gaps between the towers are tight, so the neighbouring towers look in. There are no terraces yet.

floor_changes.direction: toward the Thames to the S
floor_changes.why: Every flat gets a garden balcony facing the river, with the overhang shading the flat below.
Stepping down to the north lets the middle tower see over it.

win1.whats_wrong: A single slim slab, slightly twisted, reaching about 194 m. It is elegant, but it is a sealed glass box with no outdoor space, and it pushes above the City's grain.

floor_changes.why: Heatherwick-style greenery and outdoor space for every flat.

rows.reason: At least it tries to thread its views between the neighbours. A is a dumb box.
rows.quote: A is a filing cabinet. B has intent but no aim.

win1.whats_wrong: A plain box buried among the towers. The neighbours are closer than 20 m, so it is overlooked on every side. It has no outdoor space and no identity.

floor_changes.direction: toward the harbour to the S/SW
floor_changes.why: The only clear sight lines are toward the harbour, between the neighbouring towers.
Outdoor space, and an identity like Sanjay Puri's work.

hyb.whats_wrong: The plates rotate back and forth, so some floors do find the gaps between the neighbouring towers. The rotation looks random rather than aimed at the harbour, and it has no balconies.

floor_changes.direction: hold one rotation toward the harbour
floor_changes.why: Stop the wobble and aim the upper floors.
Outdoor space.

rows.reason: It has a calmer, more dignified silhouette and more distance from the neighbours.
rows.quote: A breathes. B fidgets.

hyb.whats_wrong: A rounded, waisted tower about 119 m tall, set in the fat corner of the triangular site. The silhouette is graceful, but the plate is the same on all sides, so the flats facing east over the open land get the same treatment as the others.

floor_changes.direction: toward the parks to the NE
floor_changes.why: Gives the flats better park views while keeping neighbours at a distance.

win1.whats_wrong: A chamfered octagon whose floors jitter in and out. It gives the tower some texture, but the effect looks arbitrary, and the lower floors overlook the slab blocks next door.

floor_changes.direction: away from the slab block to the SW
floor_changes.why: Privacy for the lower flats.
A rhythm like SHoP's work, not noise.

rows.reason: The base of B respects the street grid, and its milder twist overlooks the neighbours slightly less.
rows.quote: B is the good neighbour; now give it some gardens and let it turn properly to the water.

hyb.whats_wrong: A slim twist of about 40 degrees on a tight lot, deep in a canyon of taller neighbours. The rotation moves the corners around, but no floor actually opens toward the harbour, and the flat faces still look straight at the slab to the east.

floor_changes.direction: away from the slab tower to the east
floor_changes.amount: about 10 degrees, holding the west face parallel to the street wall
floor_changes.why: The low floors see nothing but the neighbour's windows, so angle them off it and keep the street edge calm for the heritage context.

floor_changes.amount: one 4 x 4 m double-height notch every 3 floors
floor_changes.why: This is where the harbour view clears the canyon. Give each flat a Safdie-style garden there.

win1.whats_wrong: The same tower with a gentler twist of about 25 degrees. The base squares up to the street grid, which is better for context. It is still an extrusion with no outdoor space, and the upper floors do not commit to the water.

floor_changes.direction: toward the harbour to the SW
floor_changes.why: The rotation should end on the view, not stop halfway.
Terraces on the top floors and a softer crown against the historic skyline.

rows.reason: B has the gesture that A lacks. It needs the fat taken off the head and the waist relieved.
rows.quote: B at least has a pulse; A is a well-mannered bollard in a park.

hyb.whats_wrong: A diamond-rotated square with a light taper, set in the middle of a large green plot. It is slim and simple but inert, and it does nothing for the public realm at its foot. The base is a grey plinth that sits awkwardly on the park.

floor_changes.direction: open toward the park to the south
floor_changes.amount: lift the plate on a 2-storey colonnade
floor_changes.why: The ground should belong to the park, not to a plinth.

floor_changes.direction: all sides, biased toward the river to the NE
floor_changes.why: Sharpen the silhouette and open the corners to the water.

win1.whats_wrong: A twist of about 45 degrees with a waist that narrows around floor 24 and swells again at the top. It has real skyline presence, but the mid-height pinch squeezes the plates hard. The top-heavy crown feels unresolved.

floor_changes.amount: about 2 m more per side at the waist
floor_changes.why: The waist plates are too small for decent flats.

floor_changes.direction: toward the river to the NE
floor_changes.amount: step down 2 floors on the NE corner
floor_changes.why: Resolve the swollen head into a crown facing the view.

rows.reason: B gives outdoor space with a repeatable slab edge, and A gives none.
rows.quote: Balconies sell. B has them, A doesn't. Now build it to the height we paid for.

hyb.whats_wrong: A rotated square prism of identical plates with tiny chamfer changes, about 160 m where 305 m is allowed. It is efficient but gives up height, and it has no balconies at all. Towers to the south and west crowd the lower half.

floor_changes.why: The water view is above the neighbours, and that is where the value is.

floor_changes.amount: a 3 m inset corner balcony, repeated
floor_changes.why: Gives every flat outdoor space using one repeatable detail.

win1.whats_wrong: Rounded plates with a slight shift in the upper floors and ring slab-edge balconies, which is good. The top shrinks and turns oddly. It is still well short of the allowed height.

floor_changes.amount: about 12 more floors at the floor-24 plate size
floor_changes.why: Do not shrink the top. Carry the plate up to where the water opens.
Keeps the formwork cycle efficient.

rows.reason: B's layered slabs give shade and form. A is only a box.
rows.quote: B has a skin that breathes; A is a filing cabinet.

hyb.whats_wrong: A near-square plate on the grid with small chamfers that jump from corner to corner. It reads as a mute block among the old towers, with no shading, no in-between space and no directional intent.

floor_changes.direction: toward the river to the east
floor_changes.amount: a 2-storey verandah every 4 floors, 4 m deep
floor_changes.why: Doshi's in-between space, which also blocks sightlines from the tower across the street.

floor_changes.amount: 1.5 m per floor on two faces
floor_changes.why: A tapered prism in the KPF sense, with a crown that belongs among the heritage tops.

win1.whats_wrong: Soft rounded plates with layered slab edges that step in and out. It is sculptural and shaded by the slab overhangs, but the top shrinks abruptly and the tower looks stubby against its old neighbours.

floor_changes.why: The abrupt shrink reads as an accident, not a crown.

floor_changes.direction: toward the river to the east
floor_changes.why: Turn the soft form toward the water and away from the street-wall neighbours.

rows.reason: A's pair has more weight and suits the context. B's slenderness is lovely but alien here.
rows.quote: Three pencils in Dadar is a gesture; two good towers is architecture.

win1.whats_wrong: Two chamfered towers set on a diagonal. They stand well clear of each other, but the pair reads as twins of unequal height. Both face the low Dadar fabric with no adjustment to the sea to the west, and the plinths are bare.

floor_changes.direction: toward the Arabian Sea to the west
floor_changes.why: Aim the long faces at the sea, not at each other.

floor_changes.amount: a 4-storey podium matching the chawl cornice
floor_changes.why: Ties the towers to the heritage street height.

hyb.whats_wrong: Three slim rounded towers spread to the corners. They are very slender and elegant, but three thin pencils read as foreign against Dadar's grain, and the NW tower hugs the site line.

floor_changes.amount: remove 1 tower and widen the other two by 3 m
floor_changes.why: Two proper towers sit better in the low context than three sticks.
Gives a Foster-like, refined top facing the sea.

rows.reason: B spreads the towers so each gets its own outlook. A stacks one behind the other.

win1.whats_wrong: A square plate that rotates up to about 194 m. It is slim but flat, with no outdoor space. The base meets the ground with no podium or public realm, and it looms over the historic block next door.

floor_changes.direction: open the ground to the street
floor_changes.amount: a 2-storey colonnade on the S/W edges
floor_changes.why: A generous public realm at the base.

floor_changes.direction: S corner toward the Tower and Thames
floor_changes.why: Outdoor space per flat.

hyb.whats_wrong: A soft plate on a genuine podium, looking toward the Tower of London and the Thames. It holds a better street edge. At about 115 m it is stout, and the floor edges have banding but no balconies.

floor_changes.direction: stepping toward the river to the S
floor_changes.why: Terraces facing the Tower view.
Refines the top.

rows.reason: By a narrow margin: its square plate spreads the corner views more fairly, but both are canyon-bound.
rows.quote: Both are trapped in the canyon; the only real fix is height.

hyb.whats_wrong: A diagonal rectangle held constant to about 144 m, deeply embedded among supertalls. Its long faces look straight at the neighbouring towers at close range, so flats on the NE side get no view equity. The plan is efficient.

floor_changes.direction: long faces toward the park gap to the SW
floor_changes.why: Aims the flats down the only open slot.

floor_changes.amount: use the full ~245 m allowance, +25 floors
floor_changes.why: Clears the neighbours for Central Park views.

win1.whats_wrong: A near-square plate with a slight progressive rotation. It is fairer for corner flats but still boxed in by the towers, with less efficient depth.

floor_changes.why: Turns the glazing off the neighbour's windows.
Gets above the canyon.

rows.reason: A's stronger rotation reads better on the skyline and faces the sea more squarely.
rows.quote: Nice blade; now carve Puri-style gardens into it.

win1.whats_wrong: A triangular blade that rotates from the site's tip toward the Arabian Sea. It is bold, slender and has no neighbours looking in. However, it has no balconies or sky gardens for Mumbai living, and the twist costs money.

floor_changes.why: Outdoor space and monsoon shade.

floor_changes.direction: swing the broad face toward the sea to the W
floor_changes.why: More flats directly face the sea.

hyb.whats_wrong: Almost the same blade with a gentler rotation. It is slightly less dramatic but has the same lack of outdoor space.

floor_changes.why: Outdoor rooms.
Skyline identity.

rows.reason: At least it faces the river.
rows.quote: Two extrusions; B at least knows where the Thames is.

win1.whats_wrong: A chamfered bar extruded dead-straight to 194 m with no top, no base and no gesture. It is a pencil. Its long axis points N-S, so neither long face commands the Thames. It gives nothing to the street.

floor_changes.why: Public realm.

floor_changes.direction: long face S to the Thames
floor_changes.why: The river view.
Identity.

hyb.whats_wrong: A rectangle whose long face is angled to the Thames. It frames the river properly but is still a blank extrusion with no crown or public ground.

floor_changes.why: Sculptural and view-seeking.
Street life.

rows.reason: A is softer and a little less exposed on the east. Neither design gives a flat any outdoor room.
rows.quote: Two glass sticks and not one verandah between them. This is Mumbai, not Frankfurt.

hyb.whats_wrong: A squircle plate that tapers only at the very top on a triangular plot. No balconies, no verandahs, no deep shade. It faces every direction equally when the sea is to the west and Shivaji Park is to the north. The slab tower to the east looks straight into it.

floor_changes.direction: on the W and NW corners toward the sea and the park
floor_changes.amount: double-height verandah cut 3 m deep every 2 floors
floor_changes.why: Every flat gets outdoor space and shade from the afternoon sun off the sea

floor_changes.direction: away from the slab tower to the east
floor_changes.amount: solid east face with the windows turned about 20 degrees
floor_changes.why: Stops the neighbours looking in at close range

win1.whats_wrong: A thin, taller rectangular extrusion set on the diagonal, 46 floors of the same plate. The long faces look NE and SW, not at the sea. There is nowhere to sit outside. Correa would call it a sealed box in a monsoon city.

floor_changes.direction: long face toward the sea to the west
floor_changes.why: The long frontage currently misses the Arabian Sea

floor_changes.amount: 2.5 m recessed verandahs on alternating floors
floor_changes.why: Outdoor space per flat and monsoon shading

rows.reason: B at least has a sculptural idea, and it keeps the efficient core.
rows.quote: B is whispering. Make it speak to the river.

win1.whats_wrong: A chamfered hexagonal extrusion with no gesture at all. The plan is efficient, but nothing on the Canary Wharf skyline would register it, and the massing does nothing toward the Thames views to the south and east.

floor_changes.direction: stepping down toward the Thames to the S/SE
floor_changes.why: Sky terraces give the building an identity and put the premium flats on the river

hyb.whats_wrong: The rounded plate rotates slightly and the floor edges undulate, which reads as ribbons. It has more character than A, but the move is timid and has no clear direction. It wobbles instead of committing to the river.

floor_changes.direction: rotating clockwise to open toward the river bend to the SE
floor_changes.why: Commit to the gesture and aim the upper floors at the water

floor_changes.amount: about 12 m drop across the plate
floor_changes.why: A skyline marker

rows.reason: The cruciform twist is slender and multi-aspect, and it breaks the bulk up.
rows.quote: B has a body. A is just a column of floor plates.

win1.whats_wrong: A rotated square extrusion wedged between large Lower Manhattan towers. The plate fills most of the small site, so there is no plaza or shade at the street. It stands squat against the slender towers around it.

floor_changes.direction: to the plaza on the east
floor_changes.amount: set the base back 4 m and lift it on pilotis
floor_changes.why: Give the ground back to the street, a shaded threshold in Doshi's sense
Better proportion among the tall neighbours

hyb.whats_wrong: A cruciform plate that twists up the tower. The notches give each flat several aspects and break up the bulk. The rotation looks arbitrary rather than tuned to the harbour, and the base still fills the site.

floor_changes.direction: opening the notches toward the Hudson to the W
floor_changes.amount: lock the rotation at about 15 degrees
floor_changes.why: Aim the recesses at the water, not at random
Public realm

rows.reason: B's edges suggest shading and a climate response. A is inert.
rows.quote: B could breathe. A just stands in the sun.

win1.whats_wrong: A small square prism in a large park-like site next to Shivaji Park. The tower sits in open ground, so privacy is good. The shape is blank, with no shading and no response to the westerly sea breeze.

floor_changes.direction: on the west and south faces
floor_changes.why: Shade, cross-ventilation and a vertical village in the MVRDV sense

hyb.whats_wrong: A rounded plate that tapers and undulates, with floor lips that could work as shading. It is prettier, but the plan is small and less efficient, and nothing reaches toward the sea to the west.

floor_changes.direction: toward the Arabian Sea to the W
floor_changes.why: Deep overhangs shade the west faces and frame the sea

rows.reason: A's orientation and slight top set-back do marginally better.
rows.quote: Fine, efficient, and forgettable. Give me balconies.

hyb.whats_wrong: A clean rectangular extrusion that steps in slightly at the crown. Its long face turns toward the sea to the SW, which is correct. There are no balconies.

floor_changes.direction: on the SW corner facing the sea
floor_changes.amount: 3 m deep balcony pockets on every floor
floor_changes.why: Outdoor space for each flat without hurting the plan

win1.whats_wrong: A square prism rotated to the diagonal. It is efficient, but no face addresses the sea or the park squarely.

floor_changes.direction: one face square to the sea to the W
floor_changes.why: Give the sea to more flats

rows.reason: A's podium and floor shifts give some craft to work with.
rows.quote: Neither has a hand in it. A at least has a base I can sculpt.

hyb.whats_wrong: A rotated square tower on a big podium, with slight offsets between floor bands. The podium dominates the streets. Nothing ties the building to the docks' heritage, and there is little outdoor space.

floor_changes.amount: cut the podium back by half and add a stepped public roof
floor_changes.why: A heritage waterfront scale and a public realm

floor_changes.direction: toward the Thames to the S
floor_changes.why: Outdoor terraces per flat

win1.whats_wrong: A plain square prism with no podium. It is cleaner at the ground but without any character or outdoor space.

floor_changes.amount: alternate the balcony zones in a SHoP-style patterned facade
floor_changes.why: Texture, and brick-rhythm references to the warehouse heritage

rows.reason: A is more slender and angled for privacy.
rows.quote: The evidence favours A: thinner, oblique, and it looks at the river.

win1.whats_wrong: A slim rectangular slab that rotates gently up the tower. Its long faces look roughly NE and SW, toward the Thames. The oblique angles keep neighbours from facing it squarely in the dense medieval grain. The base is heavy.

floor_changes.direction: toward the river to the S
floor_changes.why: More river from the upper flats, and it avoids the office blocks to the N

hyb.whats_wrong: A chamfered octagon, shorter and stubbier. All-round glazing exposes flats to the close office neighbours on every side.

floor_changes.direction: away from the blocks to the N and E
floor_changes.why: Privacy at the lower levels

rows.reason: The twist spreads the views more fairly, and the tower rises above the blockers.
rows.quote: B gives every flat a turn at the water.

hyb.whats_wrong: A chamfered box with ribbon floor lips on a podium that fills the triangle. The supertall neighbour to the south blocks the harbour for most flats, so view equity is poor.

floor_changes.amount: add about 25 m within the allowance
floor_changes.why: Clear the neighbouring tower and reach the harbour
Public realm

win1.whats_wrong: A triangular plate twisting up to 216 m. It is taller and more slender, and the rotation fans each face across several outlooks, which helps equity. The corners are tight.

floor_changes.why: Usable corner rooms and less wind
Street life

rows.reason: Both are slender and similarly private. A is cleaner and B is livelier.
rows.quote: Pick A's discipline or B's texture. Either is buildable.

win1.whats_wrong: A very slender square tower of about 230 m. The proportion is elegant, but the small plate is inefficient. The base is exposed to the low blocks to the NE.

floor_changes.amount: about 1 m per side every 5 floors
floor_changes.why: Refines the top and reduces wind

hyb.whats_wrong: A rectangular plate with stacked offsets and clipped corners. It is a little more lively, but the joints look fussy and they add transfer costs.

floor_changes.amount: align the offsets into three clear blocks
floor_changes.why: Clean proportion and simpler structure

rows.reason: B has the same repetition as A, but the plate faces the river and there is less diagonal overlooking.
rows.quote: B builds like a Swiss watch and actually looks at the water; now give it a crown worth the skyline.

floor_changes.direction: corner facing the river to the west
floor_changes.why: Opens a true river-facing facet and avoids looking straight into the low blocks next door

floor_changes.amount: about 20 degrees in a single step
floor_changes.why: One rotation keeps the formwork repetitive and squares the top half to the water

hyb.whats_wrong: A square rotated about 20 degrees, identical on every floor. The broad face looks up the river, which is better. The expressed floor bands read well, but the crown is mute and the east face looks straight at the dense grey block.

floor_changes.why: Gives premium terraces with a harbour view and a legible top
Screens the overlook from the east and adds a Heatherwick-like moment without breaking repetition

rows.reason: B's round plate gives fairer corner views to every flat and a more fluid silhouette.
rows.quote: B has the curvature every flat deserves; A is an octagon pretending to be a vase.

win1.whats_wrong: A chamfered octagon whose plate shrinks at mid-height and then grows again. The waist is timid, the slab edges look stacked rather than flowing, and it is stocky for 180 m. The flat corners give unequal views across the flats.

floor_changes.direction: all sides, biased toward the river
floor_changes.why: Strengthens the waist and gives mid-level flats more corner glazing
The proportion reads squat against the river

hyb.whats_wrong: The soft squircle plate spreads views evenly, and the top pinches in nicely. Below the top the floors are nearly the same, so the silhouette only moves in the last 10 floors, and the podium is a hard octagon that clashes with the tower.

floor_changes.direction: toward the river to the west
floor_changes.why: A longer, fluid taper gives more flats a crown-level view

floor_changes.amount: round the podium to match the tower
floor_changes.why: Continuity of form

rows.quote: A is a sculpture trapped at 120 m; B is 184 m of nothing. Combine them.

hyb.whats_wrong: Stacked, softly shifting squircle slabs give MAD-like identity, but it stops at about 122 m in a deep canyon of supertalls. The lower half looks straight into neighbouring walls, and the plate fills too much of the site to read as slender.

floor_changes.why: Rise above the canyon walls to get past the neighbours
Increases the distance to the adjacent towers

win1.whats_wrong: A rotated square extruded to about 184 m. The height is good, but it is a generic extrusion with no skyline identity, and the diagonal faces look into the tower to the south-east.

floor_changes.direction: toward the open avenue view to the north
floor_changes.amount: about 2 degrees per floor to 30 degrees
floor_changes.why: Adds identity and turns the upper flats off the neighbour
Makes it register on the skyline

rows.reason: A is more humane and private, but B's twist has more identity.
rows.quote: Both are close; A feels like a home, B feels like a gesture. I'd like A with a little of B's twist.

hyb.whats_wrong: A slim, rounded tower on a large podium that uses the hexagonal site well. The squircle rotates slightly as it rises, which is gentle and elegant, but there are no terraces or gardens, and the harbour-side flats get the same glass as the ones facing the dense street.

floor_changes.direction: toward the harbour to the west
floor_changes.why: Safdie-style outdoor rooms with a view
Privacy screen from the close neighbours

win1.whats_wrong: A rotating square twists nicely to about 194 m, and the top faces more toward the water. However, the sharp corners at the low floors point straight into the adjacent block, and the empty podium plaza is wasted.

floor_changes.why: Stops a corner looking into the neighbour
Gives the plaza a purpose

hyb.whats_wrong: A straight square extrusion that respects the grid and is efficient. But in the BIG sense it is a non-move: there is no gesture toward the river views along the avenue, and no setback that responds to the neighbours' heritage cornices.

floor_changes.amount: streetwall set at cornice height, about 40 m
floor_changes.why: Relate to the Midtown heritage datum

floor_changes.direction: toward the river to the east
floor_changes.why: A bold move that takes the view

win1.whats_wrong: A square twisted about 45 degrees from base to top gives real form and swings the upper plates toward the open avenue. Efficiency drops in the transition floors, and the low rotated plate breaks the street grid.

floor_changes.why: Keeps the streetwall and heritage context, and efficient low floors
Concentrates the gesture where the views are
