rows.quote: A sells the view, B sells the square metres — splay B and I'd take it.

win1.whats_wrong: A trefoil single tower gives three wings with a view each, oriented to the park and sea. It is saleable and private, but squat at about 155 m, and it leaves density on the table on a site this big.

floor_changes.why: Slenderness and a finer crown
Adds skyline identity and the highest-value units

hyb.whats_wrong: Two slim square towers with more saleable area. But they are rotated identically and parallel, so the facing facades look into each other, and the north tower shades the south one's view of the park.

floor_changes.direction: rotate the south tower 15 degrees toward the sea
floor_changes.why: Stops the two towers facing each other
Privacy

rows.reason: A's grace and privacy outweigh B's plan efficiency.
rows.quote: A is a reed at the water's edge; B is a filing cabinet with a nice view.

hyb.whats_wrong: A very slender, softly twisting cylinder at the dock edge, with an elegant Piano-like lightness. The round plate is less efficient for layouts, and the podium is a hard hexagon.

floor_changes.direction: toward the Thames to the south
floor_changes.why: Gives outdoor rooms over the river

floor_changes.direction: away from the tower to the east
floor_changes.why: Privacy from the nearby towers

win1.whats_wrong: A diamond-rotated square extrusion. It is efficient and the corners point at the water, but it is visually inert, and the corner flats on the north face look at the office cluster.

floor_changes.why: Brings more faces toward the Thames
Adds skyline presence

rows.reason: A has the height and proportion; B fits the context. Neither addresses privacy.

win1.whats_wrong: A rotated square pencil tower to about 216 m, perfectly repetitive. The diagonal faces peer into the neighbouring supertall directly to the east, and the rotation ignores the Manhattan grid.

floor_changes.why: Heritage streetwall

floor_changes.direction: away from the supertall to the east
floor_changes.why: Reduce overlooking

hyb.whats_wrong: A rectangular slab to about 151 m, aligned to the diagonal site edge, with a long face toward the open plaza, which is sensible. It is shorter and bulkier, and the long face close to the adjacent tower creates overlooking.

floor_changes.why: Clear the neighbouring mass
Proportion and distance to the neighbour

rows.reason: Both are the same timid needle.
rows.quote: Two pencils on a football pitch — give me a building that breathes toward the sea.

hyb.whats_wrong: A tiny square needle on a huge site, with a mild rotation. It is buildable, but it wastes the site and has no sculptural response to the sea to the west or Shivaji Park.

floor_changes.direction: toward the Arabian Sea to the west
floor_changes.why: Faces the sea
Skyline identity

win1.whats_wrong: A small clipped diamond with occasional notches. There is a hint of articulation, but it is still a thin stick with no idea behind it, and the corners point at the sea and park rather than opening a face to them.

rows.reason: A has a skyline identity. B is too timid.

hyb.whats_wrong: The rotating square gives Midtown a gesture, but the rotation is erratic, not continuous: floors 18, 30 and 41 flip back and forth, so it reads as a stack of shuffled trays and not one sculpted twist. floor_changes.direction: single sense, clockwise, finishing with the diagonal toward the rivers to the W/NW
floor_changes.why: A single twist carries the sculptural read and swings every corner flat toward the water in turn.

floor_changes.amount: a 5-storey colonnaded base set back 3 m
floor_changes.why: The street needs an arcade, not a bare shaft landing on it.

floor_changes.direction: open corner toward the river views
floor_changes.why: The top should be a proper skyline signature, not a shrunken plate.

win1.whats_wrong: Rectangle rotating steadily to a diagonal: a clean idea, but the rotation is too slight to register on the skyline and it reads as a plain box. The long faces still stare across the street at the neighbours.

floor_changes.direction: swing the long face toward the Hudson to the W
floor_changes.why: Make the move legible and turn the long elevation to the water, off the neighbour to the E.

Public realm.

rows.reason: B has disciplined proportion and corner-oriented views. A's rotation is noise.

floor_changes.direction: hold a steady orientation, with the corners toward the East River and the Hudson
floor_changes.amount: limit the rotation to 1 continuous 30-degree turn
floor_changes.why: This gives proportional calm and a clear pair of view diagonals.

floor_changes.direction: away from the slab tower to the SW

A finer finial for a 300 m+ tower.

win1.whats_wrong: A pure diamond extrusion. It is superbly slender and the corners point to the diagonal views, but it is completely unmodulated and has no terraces or relief for the residents.

floor_changes.direction: the N and W corner tips, toward the rivers
floor_changes.amount: a 3 m x 3 m winter garden notch every third floor
floor_changes.why: Private outdoor rooms facing the view, with privacy kept.
A refined crown.

rows.reason: The marginal skew in B helps privacy. Otherwise the two are the same.
rows.quote: The skew is the only measurable difference. Push it.

win1.whats_wrong: Three identical rounded-square cylinders strung N-S in a line. The middle tower blocks sightlines between the other two, and all three are clones, so the skyline gets a picket fence, not a cluster. The ground plane is under-used.

floor_changes.direction: tallest tower toward the Thames to the S
floor_changes.why: The cluster steps down away from the river and gives better silhouette and views.

floor_changes.direction: rotate the middle tower off the axis of its neighbours
floor_changes.why: Reduces direct face-to-face overlooking between towers.

floor_changes.direction: link along the medieval lane lines
floor_changes.why: Activates the public realm between the towers.

hyb.whats_wrong: The same three clones, slightly skewed. The rotation is small, which is evidence of some privacy thinking, but the silhouette is unchanged.

floor_changes.direction: the north and south towers splayed away from the middle one
floor_changes.why: More measurable separation of sightlines.
Skyline identity.

rows.reason: The rotation gives slightly better privacy. It is still buildable.
rows.quote: Rotate it, fine. But group the floors so the contractor can breathe.

win1.whats_wrong: A straight square extrusion on a triangular lot. It is highly buildable, but it ignores the triangle's views up the avenues and faces neighbouring slabs close by.

floor_changes.direction: point a corner up the avenue axis to the N
floor_changes.why: Views down the avenue corridor, away from the neighbours.
A BIG-style stepped move gives outdoor space and clears sightlines.

hyb.whats_wrong: Rotated and tapering slightly with height, which is better for oblique views, but the taper is so small that you pay for changing plates without a visible return.

floor_changes.direction: away from the tower to the E
floor_changes.amount: 0.5 m every 3 floors, in repeatable blocks
floor_changes.why: Increases the gap to the neighbour, using repeatable floor groups.
Repetition.

rows.reason: The Y-plan gives more facade and better view distribution, and a better ground.
rows.quote: The trefoil earns its perimeter. The box just stands there.

win1.whats_wrong: A trefoil/Y plan with three wings that spread the views well. But it is extruded unchanged for 58 floors, so there is no tapering proportion, and the podium plaza is residual space.

floor_changes.why: Slenderness toward the top.

floor_changes.direction: one wing toward the Thames to the S/SE
floor_changes.why: Brings a wing to face the river.
A covered public route through the site.

hyb.whats_wrong: A slowly rotating square shaft on a bulky octagonal podium. The podium is heavy on the public realm, and the shaft is a generic stick.

floor_changes.why: Return the ground plane to the street.
Views and identity.

rows.reason: A's rounded form shares the harbour view more equitably.
rows.quote: Every flat deserves a slice of the water. The round plan is more generous.

hyb.whats_wrong: A soft rounded plate that bulges and then shrinks at the top. The rounded corners distribute the views fairly. But the bulge at 32 is odd, and the lower floors sit behind the large tower to the S/E, so view equity is poor for them.

floor_changes.direction: toward the harbour to the SW
floor_changes.why: The lower flats get round the blocking tower.
Terraces on the view side for the top flats.

win1.whats_wrong: A square that rotates and slides upward. The top plates rotate toward the corner, but the result is a squat chunky box with sharp corners that favour some flats over others.

floor_changes.why: More corner flats get equal views.
Proportion.

rows.reason: Equally lazy, but A's plate is more efficient.
rows.quote: Two extrusions. Neither of them knows the sea is there.

win1.whats_wrong: A rounded-rectangle extrusion placed hard on the north edge. It is efficient but dumb: identical floors, nothing aimed at the Arabian Sea to the W or at Shivaji Park.

floor_changes.direction: long face toward the sea to the W
floor_changes.why: The long elevation should face the sea, not the chawls.
Heatherwick-style planted pockets for identity and shade.

hyb.whats_wrong: An irregular octagon, the same thing with facets. The faceting is not doing any work and creates awkward rooms.

floor_changes.why: Plan efficiency.
Views and outdoor space.

rows.reason: A has a softer, slimmer presence in a sensitive setting. It is marginally more marketable.
rows.quote: Neither sells balconies. Fix that before anything else.

hyb.whats_wrong: A slender rounded cylinder, nicely proportioned near St Paul's, but there is zero outdoor space and it has no orientation to the Thames to the S.

floor_changes.amount: a 2 m recessed balcony on every floor
floor_changes.why: Outdoor space sells, and the river is the view.
Public realm and revenue.

win1.whats_wrong: The rotated square gives the corners diagonal views, and the floor lines read as expressed slabs, but there are still no balconies and the upper plates barely change.

floor_changes.why: Premium terrace flats.
Public realm.

rows.reason: The rounded, rotating plate is more equitable and gets views past the neighbours.
rows.quote: In a canyon like this, if you do not terrace you do not live.

win1.whats_wrong: A square extrusion wedged among giants. Most floors stare into towers close by, and there is no outdoor space at all. The view to the harbour is only a slot.

floor_changes.direction: a corner toward the water gap to the W
floor_changes.why: Corner windows catch the slot views.
Safdie-style stacked terraces for every flat.

hyb.whats_wrong: A rounded form that rotates and shrinks upward, which is better at peering past neighbours, but it is lower and still gives no outdoor space.

floor_changes.direction: toward the water to the W
floor_changes.amount: a 2.5 m terrace alternating every 2 floors
floor_changes.why: Outdoor space and views for every flat.

floor_changes.amount: about 8 floors, to the 175 m allowance
floor_changes.why: Clear the adjacent roofs.

rows.reason: I cannot tell the two apart; both share the same in-line problem.
rows.quote: Two polite cylinders queuing for the river; only the front one gets served.

win1.whats_wrong: Two rounded, lightly stacked cylinders set N-S, one behind the other, so the northern tower blocks the southern tower's back and the southern tower screens the Thames for the northern one. Nothing in the plate turns to the river; the forms ignore the lanes and the heritage grain.

floor_changes.why: clear the Thames sightline for the rear tower and stop flats facing across 24 m

floor_changes.direction: along the site edges following the medieval lanes
floor_changes.why: hold the street wall of the City

hyb.whats_wrong: Identical to A as drawn: same stacked rounded towers in line, same blocked river view for the rear tower, same lack of a contextual base.

floor_changes.why: step the pair down toward St Paul's views and let the rear tower see over

floor_changes.direction: long face toward the Thames to the south
floor_changes.why: orient living rooms to the river

rows.reason: Taller, slimmer and the twist hints at the MAD-style organic move I want to push further.

win1.whats_wrong: A fat rounded extrusion that fills the triangle's wide end; no balconies, no sky gardens, no idea about outdoor life per flat.

floor_changes.why: every flat gets outdoor space facing the Thames
stepped terraces toward the view

hyb.whats_wrong: Slimmer, taller square with a slow twist; more elegant, but a square in a triangle wastes plan and still offers no outdoor rooms.

floor_changes.why: corners open to the south outlook and create cantilevered balconies
shared garden at the summit

rows.reason: It at least makes a move; A is a pencil.

floor_changes.direction: toward the plaza to the south
floor_changes.why: shaded public edge
